item.title: Finitely Verifiable Segmentation: Decidability for Every Tokenizer with a Finite-State Verifier
item.description: arXiv:2610.30168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A segmentation policy assigns to each byte string at most one segmentation into tokens. Call it finitely verifiable when a finite automaton over marked strings, bytes paired with boundary bits, accepts exactly the policy's own segmentations. The automaton judges a proposed segmentation and need not compute one. The paper shows what that hypothesis buys. Four questions that practice settles by folklore become decidable, whether a window certifies a token boundary, whether the boundary gap is bounded, whether a mask keeps generation completable, and whether two policies are equivalent. The last three specialize limitedness, coaccessibility and the equivalence of single-valued transducers. The first refines the synchronizing cut of code theory, and two more ask whether a certified cut, or the cuts of an inventory, let each piece scan alone. The class sits strictly between the online-scannable policies and those with regular domains, and its inner frontier is Choffrut's and decidable in polynomial time. Markings are length-preserving, so the class is exactly the rational segmentation policies, a normal form rather than a restriction, and what the decisions need is a supplied verifier. The class is closed under the operations pipelines use: composition over a labeled stage, restriction, splitting, and byte-fallback union of literal policies. Each composite inherits the six decisions, and certificates transfer between stages under four laws. Under rational, unifilar, almost surely stopping finite-state sources, each mass of the weighted section is an exact rational, and so is each rate where expected length is positive. Maximal-munch lexing, canonical byte-pair encoding and two-mode WordPiece instantiate the interface, and the munch library implements all six decisions. Every theorem carries an executable check, and every reported statistic is a program's own output.

item.title: Distributional Learning of Context-Free Languages under Fixed Finite-Semigroup Typing
item.description: arXiv:1409.6247v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study positive-data learning of context-free languages whose nonempty factors are typed by a fixed morphism $s:\Sigma^+\to S$ into a finite semigroup. A polynomial-time set-driven operator reconstructs each substitutable target from finite positive witnesses; a separate conservative learner identifies nonempty targets in Gold's sense. The encoded characteristic-data size is polynomial in grammar size and a typed shortest-yield parameter. Ordinary grammar thickness suffices when the typing is determined by a fixed prefix-suffix window and a finite-group value; for linear targets, linear grammar size alone suffices. Conversely, a fixed two-element semilattice typing yields finite targets with grammars of size and ordinary thickness both $O(n)$ that require exponentially long characteristic samples. The lower bound applies to any set-driven operator admitting characteristic samples for the fixed-typing class. Retyping closure, examples beyond fixed windows, and a Dyck-language obstruction delineate the framework's scope.
item.dc:creator: Takayuki Kuriyama

item.title: Beyond the Turing threshold: Productive grammars generate essentially undecidable languages
item.description: arXiv:2609.11385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Emil Post's productive sets are not even semi-computable, let alone computable, being thus essentially incomputable. Accordingly, formal languages whose set of words is a (completely) productive set are essentially undecidable. In this article, I elaborate on Post productivity from the viewpoint of formal language theory: I design formal grammars that emulate the construction of productive sets of natural numbers and are thus beyond Turing-decidability.
